analysis.one_liner: Lets cities and towns build their own broadband networks even when state laws forbid it.
analysis.headline: The Community Broadband Act of 2017 died in a Senate committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped states from banning cities and towns from offering their own internet service, which in many places is the only way to get a competitor to Comcast, AT&T, or the local cable company. It also set some guardrails: cities would have to publish their plans, take public input, let private companies bid, and not favor their own network over rivals. It was introduced on March 28, 2017, read once, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee — where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2019 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities where broadband is slow, expensive, or unavailable, especially in rural and low-income areas. Cities, towns, and tribes that want to build or run their own networks — as hundreds already do — would be freed from state laws written to stop them. The bill's text specifically directs providers to consider service in low-income areas. Existing ISPs and their customers could also benefit, since the bill forbids a public provider from favoring itself over competing private providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural and underserved communities wanting better internet

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars any state, local, or tribal legal requirement from prohibiting or inhibiting a government or its affiliate from serving as a public provider of telecommunications services.

It requires public providers to publish notice of their intentions, take public input, and consider private-sector bids and public-private partnerships before building a network, adding a layer of accountability.

It prohibits public providers from favoring themselves over competing providers in regulations, ordinances, rights-of-way, and other rules, protecting private competitors rather than shutting them out.
The bill directs coverage proposals to account for service to low-income areas and other demographically underserved populations.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the main cost would fall on incumbent internet and cable providers, which would face municipal competition in markets where state law currently shields them. Public networks themselves would be paid for by the cities that choose to build them, backed by the bill's requirement that local elected officials remain accountable and that federal funds not be committed if a public provider goes bankrupt.

drawbacks.text: Municipal networks are not guaranteed to succeed: publicly financed networks have failed or required bailouts in some communities, which is why the bill bars federal funds from flowing if a public provider goes bankrupt.
Critics of municipal broadband argue that city-run networks put taxpayer money at risk and that the bill's preemption overrides state and local control over how local money is spent.
Supporters acknowledged the competitive risk by writing in protections for private competitors: public providers cannot favor themselves over rivals and must let private firms bid before building.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents, the upside is potentially large — more competition for an essential service where many places have one or two providers — and the downside is limited to the cities that voluntarily choose to build and take on that risk. The cost falls mainly on incumbent providers, not on ordinary people. The bill's safeguards (public notice, bidding, no self-preference, bankruptcy protections) address the most serious objection, that public networks can fail with taxpayer money on the line.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read once and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The Community Broadband Act of 2017 was introduced in the Senate on March 28, 2017 by Sen. Cory Booker and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill's entire Senate action history is that single referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, floor vote, or House companion action appears in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress.
Because the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without the committee acting, the bill died there and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent internet and cable providers — and any state laws restricting municipal broadband — are better off because the bill died, since the status quo they benefit from was never put to a vote. Residents of communities barred by state law from building their own networks gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to measure party lines; the sponsor and its 5 cosponsors were Democrats-aligned, and the bill died in a Republican-led committee without action.

industries.note: The bill would have let municipal and tribal governments compete with them by preempting state laws that restrict public broadband networks. Where a city network offers a cheaper alternative, incumbents lose customers and pricing power; state-level restrictions are one of the tools that keeps that competition off the table.

industries.industry: State and local governments (as potential network operators)
industries.note: Cities, towns, and tribes gain the option to build their own broadband networks, but the bill attaches conditions: public notice, private-sector bidding, no self-preference over rivals, and bankruptcy safeguards. These add accountability but also constrain how a public network can be run.
